fields.label: Intro sentence
paragraphs: Rubber-bonded damper weight for cabin air extractor vents — adds mass at the flap so it stops fluttering and buzzing under airflow, without stiffening it enough to stop the vent working. Moulded and bonded to your drawing at our ISO 9001:2015 plant in Nashik.

fields.note: 40 words · replaces the template’s “Weight Rubber, A/C Vibration Extractor manufactured to order at our ISO 9001:2015 certified plant in Nashik”, which is the same sentence on all 31 pages with the name swapped. This version says what the part does before it says where it is made

fields.label: Hero spec block
rows: To your drawing — set from the flap mass and its opening pressure
Per compound datasheet, tested to ASTM D412
−40 to +140 °C in EPDM · −40 to +120 °C in neoprene
fields.note:
All six values are identical on every SKU page. Thickness and width describe sheet stock, not a moulded damper. 18 MPa is one tensile figure applied to eight different compounds — and unlike a blank, a buyer designs against it.
The temperature line matters here specifically: an extractor sits in the rear quarter panel or boot floor, open to outside air. The cold end is what governs — a damper that stiffens at −20 °C changes the flap’s opening behaviour in winter, which is when cabin misting makes venting matter most

fields.note:
Live set: Neoprene, SBR. Every compound above stays selectable — the change is that the page now says which is right for a damper and why two of them are not.
EPDM is the substantive change and it is not currently offered on this page at all. A cabin extractor is open to outside air — UV through the aperture, spray, road salt, and cold. Neoprene and SBR are what the live page offers, and SBR is the wrong answer for an open vent: it cracks under ozone.
Natural rubber also appears on none of the 31 SKU pages, including all five anti-vibration mounts, despite having the best rebound and bond strength of the eight. Ranges are from the locked homepage compound table

“Why does my car’s boot vent rattle?” is a real question with almost no good published answer — and this page can answer it, because the answer is the part. Stating the failure, the fix and the constraint is the best AEO passage available here.

sections.title: Why specifiers choose Margo
sections.chip: 4 cards stay four · all four rewritten
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Why Specifiers Choose Margo · four cards identical on all 31 pages · a 99.7% yield chip this page later calls “on request”

fields.label: Quality chip
fields.note: The production table in section 07 says first-pass yield is “On request”. One of the two is wrong and the honest one is the table. 99.7% is also the fourth quality figure on this website, alongside 0.2% field returns, 99.4% process consistency and the <1% target rejection in the company profile

fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: The flap is deliberately light so it lifts at almost no pressure — which is exactly what makes it buzz at road speed. Added mass raises its inertia so airflow pulses no longer move it.
Too much mass and the cabin stops venting; too little and the buzz stays. Mass, rubber hardness and the flap’s own opening pressure are set together — send the flap and we quote against it.
A steel mass in a moulded rubber body. The bond is what fails first if the compound is wrong — and moulding and bonding happen here, under one set of batch records.
EPDM, −40 to +140 °C. The extractor is open to outside air, and a damper that crazes under ozone or stiffens in the cold changes how the flap behaves.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change, and no new element added to the section. Each live card is a title plus one line, and the replacement keeps that shape exactly; only the words change.
The four live titles are identical on all 31 pages and say nothing about any part. “Superior Durability”, “Precision Tolerance”, “Global Compliance”, “Custom Formulation” would sit unchanged on a gasket, an oil seal or a floor mat. This is the only block on the page that can carry a per-part argument, and it currently carries none.
Card 01 is the one that makes the page findable. Nobody searches for “weight rubber” — people search for the noise. An NVH engineer chasing a rear-end buzz at 80 km/h is exactly the reader this part is for, and naming the failure is what puts the page in front of them.
Card 03 is the one that converts. Most Indian moulders subcontract rubber-to-metal bonding; an OEM that has had a bond-line failure knows what in-house bonding is worth.
Card 04 corrects a live selection error — see section 03. The page offers SBR, and SBR crazes under ozone at an open vent.
Cross-link: the mating part is /products/pads-stoppers-caps/ac-flaps, the extractor flap itself. It belongs in section 10, not here

notes: This is the page’s AEO asset. Everything else is shared with 30 other URLs; this block is what makes the page worth indexing separately.

Moulding process, named per part: compression moulded with the steel mass bonded in — or transfer moulded, which is the better process for an insert and is what section 06 should name here. The template names “compression moulding” on all 31 pages, which is right on most and wrong on seven.
Link “rubber-to-metal bonding” to /products/anti-vibration-mounts, which carries the bonding detail.
Never publish a metric the same page later declines to give.

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps, accurate — the best-built section on the template

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. Damping is set here — a vibration weight works by turning movement into heat, so the compound is chosen for loss rather than for bounce.
Mould design & CNC — precision steel tooling manufactured in-house and held as a controlled record. [no change — the strongest sentence in the template]

Moulding — injection, compression or transfer, selected for the part geometry. For this part: transfer moulded with the steel mass bonded in — transfer is the correct process for a part with an insert, and it is one of the three Margo runs.
Post-cure & trimming — oven post-cure for dimensional stability, followed by flash trimming. [no change]
Quality inspection — dimensional check, hardness testing and batch sampling before release. [no change]

Export packaging — industrial packing with documentation for international shipping. Bonded assemblies are packed so the metal mass cannot swing against the rubber in transit. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept — only step 03 changes materially. This section is accurate and describes work Margo actually does.
Step 02 is the strongest sentence in the whole template: “precision steel tooling manufactured in-house and held as a controlled record” is exactly what separates a manufacturer from a trading house, stated without an adjective. On this part it matters twice, because the bonded insert makes tooling control a bond-quality question too

notes: Numbered steps are an <ol>. The order is the process.
Identical on 31 pages — consider lifting it to /products and linking, which would cut ~1,050 px of duplicate content from every SKU page.
“Held as a controlled record” is audit language and it is the phrase a Tier-1 supplier questionnaire uses. Keep it.
